title: EscrowFinish fulfillment fees: XRP drops and SGD prices in the app
abstract: Measured Testnet costs and accounting: how XRP drops differ from the SGD price shown in the app, including principal and fees.
tags: EscrowFinish fulfillment fees and XRP drops
body:
EscrowFinish with a fulfillment cost 423 drops in our observed XRPL Testnet conditional finish, more than a plain XRP Payment. EscrowCreate used 12 drops, so the measured purchase overhead was 435 drops before a separate answer anchor. These are historical observations rather than a promise about future network load. A price displayed in SGD is an application accounting unit; it is not the network fee and it is not a market exchange rate.

Conditional finish costs more than a Payment. The XRPL fee formula scales as base_fee × (33 + fulfillment_bytes / 16) before multisign/load effects. Here K is 32 bytes and its encoded fulfillment is 36 bytes. At the observed 12-drop signing base, ceil(12 × (33 + 36/16)) = 423 drops. A 2,000-drop cap rejects excessive fees. Live create/cancel each cost 12 drops. A cancelled 60,000-drop principal is fully returned; its buyer still pays 24 drops in fees. - Synthetic corpus and extractive fixture answers in the proof are labelled; Testnet value transfer is real Testnet execution, with no real value.

Live purchase activity and receipts show validated create and finish links, the publication ledger, and separate policy results for key/Condition binding and ciphertext authentication/decryption. A pending CancelAfter countdown is advisory; only a validated EscrowCancel reports principal returned. Historical receipts without the new check fields do not acquire check marks by inference.

A failed signed passage promise can be challenged after EscrowFinish. Policy reopens the authenticated envelope privately; no failed plaintext enters a grant, snapshot or model. The publisher validates its recorded finish before recording the settlement for the existing record of the original refund. The refund is a separate Payment whose InvoiceID is the finish hash. Replacement expertise uses a new intent and escrow; gross budget authorization is not replenished by the refund. Each purchase keeps an identity that distinguishes its writer, article version and authorized purpose.

An envelope that cannot authenticate/decrypt, or lacks a failed passage claim, cannot support the passage challenge and remains quarantined and charged. Unsupported escrow writers remain skipped with no exact-payment fallback. Caller hire funding, royalties, change and refunds remain explicit Payments; they are transfers rather than purchases of encrypted article delivery. Offline demonstrations use labelled simulated transactions.

A refund after successful key publication is a separate writer-signed Payment. The ledger does not decide whether prose is useful, truthful or worth its price. A signed passage promise and a verifiable fraud proof establish responsibility for a broken commitment, but a real writer could refuse a refund. The fixture writer cooperates in our demonstrations. This limitation belongs beside the transaction evidence so that a reader does not mistake a cooperative recovery for unilateral buyer protection.
